definition: In computer vision, the trifocal tensor (also tritensor) is a 3×3×3 array of numbers (i.e., a tensor) that incorporates all projective geometric relationships among three views.
details: It relates the coordinates of corresponding points or lines in three views, being independent of the scene structure and depending only on the relative motion (i.e., pose) among the three views and their intrinsic calibration parameters. Hence, the trifocal tensor can be considered as the generalization of the fundamental matrix in three views. It is noted that despite the tensor being made up of 27 elements, only 18 of them are actually independent. There is also a so-called calibrated trifocal tensor, which relates the coordinates of points and lines in three views given their intrinsic parameters and encodes the relative pose of the cameras up to global scale, totalling 11 independent elements or degrees of freedom. The reduced degrees of freedom allow for fewer correspondences to fit the model, at the cost of increased nonlinearity.

explainer.lead: The trifocal tensor is a 3×3×3 array of numbers that incorporates all projective geometric relationships among three views. It matters as the three-view generalization of the fundamental matrix.

tiers.eli5: It's a compact set of numbers that captures how three photos of the same scene relate to each other, without needing to know what is in the scene.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use it to relate corresponding points or lines across three views; it depends only on relative motion among the views and intrinsic calibration, not scene structure.
tiers.paperLevel: The trifocal tensor is a 3×3×3 array relating coordinates of corresponding points or lines in three views, depending only on relative pose and intrinsic calibration; of its 27 elements only 18 are independent, and a calibrated trifocal tensor also exists.

explainer.example: Given three views of a scene, corresponding points across the images are related through the tensor's 18 independent elements.
